title: Juniper and the Atlas
premise: In 1918, Odile Sandoval drives for suffragist Marguerite Vasseur and quietly reads the letters he delivers, keeping himself small and useful. When a wounded stranger arrives carrying letters in the unmistakable hand of Henri Delacroix—a man officially dead, and now branded an enemy collaborator—Odile recognizes the handwriting of the soldier whose promise he made in peacetime: to deliver a final letter to Henri's estranged sister, whatever the cost. As the armistice negotiations stall and suspicion falls on Marguerite's household, Odile must choose between invisibility and loyalty. He delivers the letter at last, exposing both Henri's survival and his own years of quiet interception, and finds that belonging was never something he could hide his way into—it had to be claimed.
about_author: Kestrel Nystrom is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing wartime correspondence in provincial French collections. They write historical fiction about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Weight of Other People's Words
chapters.summary: Odile Sandoval's POV. We meet him driving suffragist Marguerite Vasseur through Lyon, delivering her mail—and reading every letter first, a habit born of self-protection. Emotional beat: the comfort and loneliness of being invisible, always watching other lives through paper.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Service Entrance
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. A gaunt, feverish man appears at the kitchen door asking for 'the driver who reads.' He carries a bundle of letters in handwriting Odile knows intimately: Henri Delacroix, declared dead at Verdun. Beat: dread cracking open routine; the past knocking.

chapters.title: What Was Promised in Peacetime
chapters.summary: Flashback woven into present, Odile's POV. In 1913, Henri—then a lodger—made Odile swear to deliver one sealed letter to his sister Camille if anything happened. Odile never did. Beat: guilt surfacing; the promise as debt.

chapters.title: Marguerite's War
chapters.summary: Marguerite Vasseur's POV. She fights for the vote while managing rationing, raids, and a household she suspects is hiding something. Beat: her sharp competence and isolation; power as a thing constantly defended.

chapters.title: The Handwriting of a Dead Man
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The stranger, Luc, reveals Henri is alive but trapped in occupied territory, sending letters through smugglers—and one names Odile by habit, not name. Beat: fear of exposure warring with the pull of the promise.

chapters.title: Camille Delacroix
chapters.summary: Camille's POV. A nurse running a clinic, hardened against the brother who abandoned her. She receives an unsigned note hinting Henri lives and dismisses it as cruelty. Beat: grief armored over with anger.

chapters.title: Letters That Never Arrived
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. He confesses to himself how many letters he has read, rerouted, or quietly destroyed over five years—including two from Henri before Verdun. Beat: shame deepening; the reader becomes the censored.

chapters.title: The Prefect's Men
chapters.summary: Luc's POV. Police begin asking about smuggled correspondence; collaboration charges are being drafted before the armistice is even signed. Luc decides Odile must move the final letter now. Beat: the clock starting; law ahead of peace.

chapters.title: An Argument About Votes and Silence
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She confronts Odile about his evasiveness; their argument about silence—political versus personal—mirrors each other's secrets. Beat: wary respect forming between employer and driver.

chapters.title: The Route Through Bresse
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. He plans the delivery under cover of a suffrage speaking tour Marguerite agrees to lend him. Beat: purpose replacing paralysis; hands busy again, but honestly this time.

chapters.title: Checkpoint
chapters.summary: Luc's POV. On the road, gendarmes search the car; Odile hides the letter inside a bundle of Marguerite's pamphlets, betting on their unimportance. Beat: terror and dark comedy; the cause literally shielding the promise.

chapters.title: Camille Refuses
chapters.summary: Camille's POV. Odile reaches her clinic; she recognizes nothing in him and everything in the handwriting, then refuses the letter unread. Beat: rejection as wound; inheritance of grievance.

chapters.title: What Henri Actually Wrote
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Unable to leave it, Odile breaks his own rule and reads the letter: not apology but testimony—Henri witnessed something about a local official's profiteering, and named names. Beat: the letter transforms from family matter to dangerous evidence.

chapters.title: Enemy Before the Armistice
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. News breaks that Henri, alive, will be charged as a collaborator; Marguerite realizes her household is implicated and must decide whether to protect Odile or herself. Beat: power's corruption tempting even the principled.

chapters.title: The Official in Question
chapters.summary: Luc's POV. The accused official is the same man pressuring police about smuggled mail; the charges against Henri are retaliation. Luc is detained. Beat: conspiracy tightening; allies vanishing.

chapters.title: Bargaining with Marguerite
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. He tells Marguerite everything—the reading, the promise, the letter. She weighs her reputation and chooses, conditionally, to help. Beat: confession as costly belonging; trust extended but not given freely.

chapters.title: Publication
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She prints the letter's contents in her movement's newsletter, gambling that public outrage will shield them all. Beat: audacity; using her hard-won platform as a weapon.

chapters.title: The Raid
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Police raid the house; Odile is arrested carrying nothing incriminating but confessing anyway to shield Marguerite. Beat: sacrifice; invisibility deliberately surrendered.

chapters.title: Cell and Testimony
chapters.summary: Camille's POV. Camille, finally reading the letter, comes forward to corroborate Henri's account, testifying beside the imprisoned driver she once turned away. Beat: reconciliation begun through action, not words.

chapters.title: Armistice
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. Bells ring as the armistice is signed; the official's fraud collapses; charges dissolve. Henri's fate remains uncertain across the lines. Beat: relief shadowed by unfinished business.

chapters.title: The Man Who Read Everything
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Released, Odile expects dismissal; instead Marguerite offers him real work—not driving but handling correspondence openly, his skill finally legitimate. Beat: belonging earned, not hidden into.

chapters.title: Juniper and the Atlas
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Odile's POV. Spring 1919: Henri returns diminished but alive; Camille meets him at the gate. Odile plants juniper by the door and keeps one letter unread—his own, addressed to no one, a record of who he chose to be. Beat: quiet resolution; inheritance redefined as chosen.
